virtue of the conditions of the contract of insurance indicated by the policy.
22.To repeat, the effect of the above provisions is this: when a valid insurance policy
has been issued in respect of a vehicle as evidenced by a certificate of insurance the
burden is on the insurer to pay to the third parties, whether or not there has been any
breach or violation of the policy conditions. But the amount so paid by the insurer to
third parties can be allowed to be recovered from the insured if as per the policy
conditions the insurer had no liability to pay such sum to the insured.

Insurance Company Limited v. Kokilaben Chandravadan, (1987) 2 SCC 654. Though
the said decision related to the corresponding provisions of the predecessor Act

now as the corresponding provisions are materially the same as in the Act. Learned
Judge pointed out that the insistence of the legislature that a motor vehicle can be
used in a public place only if that vehicle is covered by a policy of insurance is not for
the purpose of promoting the business of the insurance company but to protect the
members of the community who become suffers on account of accidents arising from
the use of motor vehicles.

decree passed in favour of the third party was statutory. It approved the decision in Sohan Lal Passi,

"73. The liability of the insurer is a statutory one. The liability of the insurer to satisfy
the decree passed in favour of a third party is also statutory.
              xxxx           xxxx                  xxxx     xxxx       xxxx
              xxxx           xxxx                  xxxx     xxxx       xxxx
105. Apart from the reasons stated hereinbefore, the doctrine of stare decisis
persuades us not to deviate from the said principle."
25. This Court in MAC APP. No.329/2010 Oriental Insurance Company Limited v. Rakesh Kumar
and Others and other Appeals decided by a common judgment dated 29.02.2012, noticed some
divergence of opinion in National Insurance Company Limited v. Kusum Rai & Ors., (2006) 4 SCC
250, National Insurance Company Limited v. Vidhyadhar Mahariwala & Ors., (2008) 12 SCC 701;
Ishwar Chandra & Ors. v. The Oriental Insurance Company Limited & Ors., (2007) 10 SCC 650 and

owner or driver, as the case may be.
26. The driver and owner of the offending vehicle have not challenged the finding of the Claims

Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and

payload.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Full Bench held that when a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
payload.ratio: Pursuant to the mandate of Section 149(1) and (4) of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment or award as a judgment debtor and recover the amount from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.

the compensation.

compulsory coverage of risks of third parties and other classes of persons stated therein or a policy
covering other risks by specific contract being entered into in that regard and where additional
premium is paid by the insured i.e., a contractual policy.

condition which is the cause for the accident) and the insurer proves the said breach in view of the
mandate under Section 149(1) of the Act. But, no such order can be passed against the insurer, if, on

which is enumerated under Section 149(2) of the Act or any other condition of the policy if the
Insurance Company has waived breach of any such condition or has taken the special responsibility

payload.holding: The Court held that while an attached trailer/trolley is part of an insured tractor and does not require separate insurance, the insurance company is absolved from liability because the tractor was being used to transport bricks and iron rods for construction rather than for agricultural purposes, violating the insurance policy terms.
payload.ratio: A trailer attached to a tractor is considered part of the tractor and does not require separate insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act; however, if the tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.

other purpose including the construction of a room. Thus, there is a violation of the terms and

args.question: What precedents could the insurance company use AGAINST our client, where the driver had no valid licence? Assess how damaging each one is.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. However, the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner (pay-and-recover).
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: driver had no licence at all. The tribunal found fundamental breach but ordered pay-and-recover to protect the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest precedent on facts — no licence whatsoever. It confirms the claimant will get paid, but the insurer gets recovery rights against the owner. The insurer will cite it to argue breach is fundamental.
supporting.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to satisfy third-party awards even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Invalid driving licence case. The Delhi High Court confirmed the insurer must pay third parties and recover from the owner/driver.
supporting.why_it_matters: Strong authority for the proposition that the claimant gets paid regardless of the licence defect. The insurer will cite it to establish the breach, but the ratio supports the claimant's right to payment.
supporting.quote: In view of the above discussion, there is no manner of doubt that the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Even if a fundamental breach of policy conditions is proved, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured, unless fraud or collusion is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench of Karnataka High Court — binding authority that pay-and-recover applies even for fundamental breaches like no licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most comprehensive statement of the law in the corpus. It confirms the claimant's right to payment even in the worst-case breach scenario.
supporting.quote: The Insurer is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149 (2), even if it is a fundamental breach.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had no valid licence. The court applied S. Iyyapan and directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the consistent line of authority that the third-party claimant is protected.
supporting.quote: The Hon'ble Supreme Court... has held that even if the offending vehicle was being driven by the driver having no valid driving license, insurer is liable to pay compensation to the claimants and further insurer has a right to recover the amount of compensation from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence has lapsed and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the driver does not hold a valid licence on the date of accident, but the insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Expired licence case — analogous to no valid licence. The court directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the insurer proves the licence was invalid, the third-party claimant still gets paid.
supporting.quote: The liability is fastened on the owner of the offending Maruthi Omni Car, however, the Insurance Company is directed to pay the awarded sum to the claimants and then to recover the said sum from the insured in the same proceedings by applying the principle of 'Pay and Recover'.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle, if the driver held a valid LMV licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: Supreme Court held that even if there is a licence defect (missing endorsement), the insurer must pay third parties.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the Supreme Court's most recent and authoritative statement in the corpus on the insurer's liability to third parties despite licence defects. The insurer will try to distinguish it (missing endorsement vs no licence), but the ratio on statutory liability is broad.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The Swaran Singh pay-and-recover principle applies ONLY to third-party risks under Section 149. It does NOT apply to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that if our client's claim is for OWN damage (comprehensive policy claim for vehicle damage, not third-party injury/death), the insurer has NO liability at all — not even pay-and-recover. The Supreme Court expressly held that Swaran Singh has no application to non-third-party claims.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable if our client's claim is a third-party claim (injury/death to a person). The Supreme Court in Laxmi Narain Dhut itself drew a sharp distinction: for third-party risks, the insurer must pay and recover; for own-damage claims, the insurer is completely exonerated. If our client is a third-party claimant (not the owner claiming own damage), this case actually supports our position. We must confirm the nature of the claim.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks. ... In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that the breach is 'fundamental' — meaning the owner was grossly negligent in allowing an unlicensed driver. This strengthens the insurer's case for recovery rights and may influence the tribunal to impose the full burden on the owner rather than the insurer. It also supports the insurer's argument that the owner acted wilfully, which could affect the scope of recovery.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The tribunal still ordered pay-and-recover — the claimant got paid. The finding of 'fundamental breach' affects the owner's liability to reimburse the insurer, not the claimant's right to receive compensation. The claimant's position is that the insurer must pay first; the fight over 'fundamental breach' is between the insurer and the owner.
adverse.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: Where a driver lacks a mandatory special endorsement (e.g., for hazardous goods), there is a breach of policy conditions entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that any licence defect — even a missing endorsement — constitutes a breach. The principle extends to 'no licence' cases by analogy: if a missing endorsement is a breach, then having no licence at all is certainly a breach.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still ordered pay-and-recover — the claimants were paid. The case actually supports the claimant's right to payment. The breach finding only affects the insurer's recovery rights against the owner.
adverse.quote: Therefore, the insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
adverse.principle: Where the driver had an LMV/transport licence but no specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle, the insurer must pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that licence-type mismatches are breaches. By extension, having no licence at all is an even more serious breach. The case also discusses Ram Babu Tiwari where the Supreme Court held the insurer not liable when the licence had expired and was not renewed for 3 years.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still ordered pay-and-recover. The Ram Babu Tiwari case cited within it (where the insurer was exonerated) involved a licence that had expired 3 years prior — a very different situation from a driver who never had a licence. The ratio of Chennamma itself supports pay-and-recover for third-party claims.
adverse.quote: In the present case the vehicle involved in the accident is a 'heavy goods vehicle'. The driver had licence to drive 'light motor vehicle/transport vehicle'. He did not have a valid driving licence to drive 'heavy goods vehicle'.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
adverse.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the required badge/authorisation, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that licence defects (including no licence) constitute breaches. The case also discusses the insurer's burden of proof — the insurer successfully discharged it here, which the insurer will use to argue that if they prove the breach, they get recovery rights.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court ordered pay-and-recover — the claimant was paid. The case supports the claimant's right to payment. The breach finding only matters for the insurer's recovery against the owner.
adverse.quote: The Appellant - Insurer has proved the defence as to breach or violation of policy conditions... pay and recover from the owner can be ordered.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Driving without a licence can be treated as contributory negligence, reducing the claimant's compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that if our client (the claimant) was driving without a licence at the time of the accident, the compensation should be reduced for contributory negligence. In Kamal, the tribunal deducted 50% because the injured rider had no licence and no helmet.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This applies only if our client was the driver of the vehicle (not a passenger or pedestrian). If our client was a third party (e.g., pedestrian, passenger in another vehicle), contributory negligence does not arise from the other driver's lack of licence. We must establish the factual position of our client.
adverse.quote: The contributory negligence of injured is proved in view of testimony of PW−1 Kamal who categorically deposed... he did not have DL at the time of accident... 50 % of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

adverse.title: Reserved On: 21.07.2025 vs State Of H.P
adverse.principle: The absence of a driving licence does not in itself constitute rashness or negligence in driving. However, driving without a licence is an offence under Section 181 MV Act.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that the driver's lack of licence is a statutory violation, reinforcing the breach argument. However, the main holding (no presumption of negligence from lack of licence) actually helps the claimant by severing the causal link between the licence defect and the accident.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a criminal revision, not a civil compensation case. The principle that 'no licence ≠ negligence' actually helps the claimant — the insurer must still prove that the accident was caused by the driver's negligence, not just that the driver had no licence.
adverse.quote: The accused cannot be held to be negligent merely because he did not possess any driving licence.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a passenger is carried for hire/reward in a private vehicle, the insurer is completely exonerated — no pay-and-recover order can be passed because the risk is not covered by the Act policy.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may try to analogise: if the risk (gratuitous passenger) is not covered at all, the insurer has no liability. They might argue that if the driver had no licence, the risk was never one the insurer agreed to cover, and therefore no pay-and-recover should apply.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about the TYPE of risk (gratuitous passenger) not being covered by the Act at all — a fundamentally different issue from a licence breach. The Supreme Court in Swaran Singh and S. Iyyapan has consistently held that licence breaches do NOT take the risk outside the scope of Section 147 coverage; the insurer must still pay third parties. Sukumarbai is distinguishable on this basis.
adverse.quote: The Tribunal erred in passing an order of 'pay and recover' against the insurance company when passengers travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward are not third parties.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: For gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles (risk not covered by statute or policy), the Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4)/(5) to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: Similar to doc_028 — the insurer may argue by analogy that if the risk is outside the scope of the policy, no pay-and-recover can be ordered. They might argue that an unlicensed driver creates a risk that was never underwritten.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Same as doc_028. The Supreme Court in Swaran Singh and S. Iyyapan has consistently held that licence breaches are within the scope of Section 149(2) defences — the insurer can raise them as defences but must still pay third parties. Gratuitous passenger cases are about risks NOT covered by Section 147 at all — a different legal basis.
adverse.quote: In cases where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the terms of the insurance policy... the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 149... are not attracted.

priority_arguments: 1. The claimant is a third party and the insurer's statutory liability under Section 149 MV Act is unaffected by the driver's lack of a licence — the insurer must pay and recover (S. Iyyapan, Satto, Yallavva, Meena).
2. The absence of a driving licence does not constitute negligence per se — the insurer must still prove the accident was caused by the driver's negligence (State of H.P. v. ...).
3. Even if the breach is 'fundamental', the third-party claimant's right to payment is protected — the fight over breach is between the insurer and the owner (Sunil Shreesail Killiket, Yallavva FB).
4. If the claim is for third-party injury/death (not own damage), Laxmi Narain Dhut actually supports the claimant — it limits the insurer's complete exoneration to own-damage claims only.
strategy.compensation_range: Cannot estimate without specific facts (age, income, dependents). Use compute_quantum tool with actual figures.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Quantum will be computed under Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework once the client's age, income, and number of dependents are provided. The licence issue does not affect the quantum calculation — it only affects who pays (insurer pays first, then recovers from owner).
risks: HIGH RISK — Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031): If the claim is for OWN DAMAGE (vehicle damage under a comprehensive policy), the insurer has NO liability at all. Confirm the nature of the claim immediately.

HIGH RISK — Kamal (doc_009): If our client was the driver of the vehicle and had no licence, the tribunal may deduct 50%+ for contributory negligence. Establish whether our client was driver, passenger, or pedestrian.
MEDIUM RISK — Sukumarbai (doc_028) / Mahesh Kanubhai (doc_029): The insurer may argue that no pay-and-recover should apply. This is distinguishable but the argument will be made.

MEDIUM RISK — The insurer will inevitably argue 'fundamental breach' to maximise their recovery rights against the owner. This does not affect the claimant's payment but may complicate settlement dynamics if the owner is impecunious.
LOW RISK — The insurer may argue that the owner acted wilfully (knowingly hiring an unlicensed driver), which could affect the scope of recovery. This is between insurer and owner, not the claimant.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal. Seek a direction that the insurer pay the awarded compensation to the claimant in the first instance with liberty to recover from the owner. If the claimant was a pedestrian/passenger (not the driver), emphasise that no contributory negligence arises from the other driver's lack of licence.

caveats: This corpus does not contain any case where the insurer was completely exonerated solely because the driver had no licence in a third-party claim. Every third-party claim case in this corpus resulted in pay-and-recover. The only complete exoneration cases (doc_028, doc_029, doc_014) involve gratuitous passengers — a different legal issue.
Doc_002 (Liyakat Ali) is about tractor use for non-agricultural purposes — not about licence defects. Not relevant.
Doc_007 (Harpreet Singh) is about entitlement of non-dependent legal representatives — not about licence issues.
Doc_038, 051, 054 are from unrelated areas of law (consumer dispute, criminal quashing, specific performance) — not relevant.
Doc_016 and doc_017 are criminal cases about rash/negligent driving — they establish that lack of licence ≠ negligence, which helps the claimant, but they are not civil compensation precedents.

The corpus does not contain any judgment where the Supreme Court overruled or limited S. Iyyapan. The law as per this corpus is that S. Iyyapan (pay-and-recover for licence defects in third-party claims) remains good law.

1. This is an appeal in a Motor Accident Claim case.
2. Heard. I have perused the record.
3. On 29.09.2007, S. Amarjeet Singh (hereinafter the deceased) was travelling from Kishtwar to
Jammu by a car bearing registration No. JK0 2D-9212. Respondent No. 3, Inderjit Singh Bali, who
was owner of the car, was on the wheel. The car met with an accident near a place called Thathri and
plunged into a trench. Deceased suffered grievous injuries. He died.
4. Respondent Nos. 1 & 2, (hereinafter the claimants) who are the sons of the deceased, filed a claim
for compensation under section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1998 (hereinafter the Act) before the
Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Jammu (hereinafter the Tribunal) against the owner and insurer
(herein appellant) of the offending car.
5. Learned Tribunal vide its judgment and award dated 30.04.2010 found that the accident had
occurred due to rash and negligent driving by respondent No. 3 and awarded compensation of Rs.

5. Learned Tribunal vide its judgment and award dated 30.04.2010 found that the accident had
occurred due to rash and negligent driving by respondent No. 3 and awarded compensation of Rs.

17,53,800/ to claimants. The Tribunal foisted liability of paying the compensation on the appellant.

deceased was a Government servant serving as Manager QC in the Food Corporation of India. His
monthly salary was Rs. 24,149/. He was aged 54 years as at the time of his death. Learned Tribunal
deducted 1/3rd of the salary towards personal expenses of the deceased and took the remaining Rs.
16,100/ as his monthly contribution towards the claimants. Annual contribution of the deceased
towards the claimants thus came out as Rs. 1, 93,200/, which became the 'multiplicand' for
calculating compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'. On the basis of the age of the
deceased, applicable multiplier being 11, learned Tribunal scaled it down to 9. Compensation under
this head thus amounting to Rs. 17, 38, 800/ (1, 93,200x9). In addition, learned Tribunal awarded
Rs. 15,000/ as compensation for funeral expenses. Total compensation thus awarded was Rs. 17,
53,800/.

the extent of the quantum of compensation awarded to the claimants. Award has been assailed on
the ground that only respondent No. 2, who is a MBA student, should have been taken as dependent
of the deceased, whereas respondent No. 1 could not have been because he is gainfully employed as
per the evidence available before the Tribunal. It is also contended that as per the evidence, the
basic salary of the deceased was Rs. 10,600/ and the total amount which he was drawing after
deduction was Rs. 19,481/. It is also contended that both the claimants were major but this aspect
was ignored by the learned Tribunal.

21. Judgment in Smt. Lalitha (supra) relied upon by learned respondent's counsel (supra) would not
apply to this case and does not lay down a different principle. Situation in that case was not one
where claimant was not dependent on the deceased at the time of his death. The claimant rather had
got compassionate appointment in place of the deceased and the High Court of Karnataka had held
that income earned by the claimant was in lieu of services rendered by him, which cannot be
adjusted against the compensation for loss of dependency. Likewise, judgment in Kulsum Bhai has
no application to this case as question involved therein was altogether different.

compensation under the head 'loss of dependency' is discernible from the judgment of the Supreme

files an application for compensation, the quantum cannot be less than the liability

the claimant if he or she is a legal representative will be entitled to compensation, the

Act. The appeal is allowed to the aforesaid extent. There will be no order as to
costs...."
23. The legal position, thus, can be summarized that a legal representative of a victim of a motor
accident, who was not dependent upon the deceased, though can lay a claim for compensation, he is
not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'. He would be entitled to

o
costs...."
23. The legal position, thus, can be summarized that a legal representative of a victim of a motor
accident, who was not dependent upon the deceased, though can lay a claim for compensation, he is
not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'. He would be entitled to

compensation for loss to estate as well as the statutory compensation under section 140 of the Act.
24. Having stated the legal position as above, it can be said that learned Tribunal has erred in taking
respondent (claimant) Harpreet Singh too as a claimant entitled to get compensation under the
head 'loss of dependency' and in that taking strength of the family of the deceased as three and
deducting 1/3rd of the salary towards personal expenses of the deceased. Claimant-Harpreet Singh,
though a legal representative of the deceased and thereby entitled to lay the claim for compensation,
is not entitled to get compensation under the head 'loss of dependency' for the reason that he is
gainfully employed in Central Government service and was not dependent upon the deceased .
25. Strength of the family of the deceased for the purpose of 'loss of dependency' in this case should
have been and is being taken as two only and in applying the multiplier method, deduction towards
personal expenses of the deceased would be half of the salary. Since the deceased at the time of the
death was 50 plus, no addition to the income of the deceased is to be made. However, given that
total annual salary of the deceased was Rs. 2, 89,788/ (29149 x 12) and his savings, earning
deduction from taxable income was Rs. 52,224/ only so at least Rs. 15,000/ can be and should have
been deducted towards income tax. Effective income of the deceased should have been and is being
taken as Rs. 2, 74,788/- (2,89,788-15,000). Personal expenses of the deceased and his contribution
towards claimant-Harbaksh Singh for calculating compensation therefore, would be Rs. 1,37,394/
say Rs. 1,37,400/ each (half of Rs. 2,74,788/) each. This would be the 'multiplicand' in this case.
26. Deceased at the time of death was in the age group of 50 to 55. Applicable multiplier as per Sarla
Verma's case (supra) is 11.

payload.holding: The High Court held that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation for the death of a gratuitous passenger carried in a goods vehicle, dismissed the owners' appeal regarding negligence and quantum, and dismissed the claimants' cross-objections for enhancement.

1. This order shall also dispose of the Misc. Appeal No. 55 of 1981 filed by the Insurer against the one
and the same award dated 17-11-.1980 passed by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal Ratlam in
Claim Case No. 16 of 1977.
2. It may be stated at the outset that the appeal No. 26 of 1981 is by the owners of the accident
vehicle and the other appeal is by the insurer. The claimants have filed cross-objections.
3. For the purpose of these appeals it is no longer in controversy that the tractor bearing
Registration No. MPU 5571 belonging to Shivlal and Kanhaiyalal (the appellants in appeal No.
26/81) was involved in an accident and had turned turtle at about 11.30 a.m. on 24-4-77 on the road
between Bibdod and Ratlam ahead of the culvert from Sagod. At the time of the accident the vehicle
was being driven by Shivlal and was insured (vide Ex. P/3) with the appellant in M. A. No. 55/81.
Laxminarayan an agriculturist aged about 50 years who was travelling by the tractor which had been
brought to his field in connection with the boring of well there had met instant death as a result of
the accident. The respondent Rukmabai is the widow of the said Laxminaryan and the minor
respondents Radheshyam and Jagdish are his sons.
4. According to the petition, the accident had occurred due to the negligence of Shivlal who at the
relevant time was driving the tractor at excessive speed and had lost control over it when he was
faced with a cow on the road. It was stated in the petition that the deceased was an agriculturist and
also a milk vendor and used to make a net income of Rs. 5,000/- per year and looking to the history
of longevity in the family, he would have lived up to the age of 90 years. Claim for compensation was

12. It is pertinent to point out that immediately after the accident Shivlal had lodged a report of the

13. It is well settled that the liability for compensation is founded on negligence. Normally from the

presumed in each and every case. Therefore, normally it is for the claimants to prove negligence. But
there is an exception to this normal rule. Where the accident is such that it attracts the doctrine of

args.question: What precedents could the insurance company use AGAINST our client, where the driver had no valid licence? Assess how damaging each one is.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. However, the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner (pay-and-recover).
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: driver had no licence at all. The tribunal found fundamental breach but ordered pay-and-recover to protect the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest precedent on facts — no licence whatsoever. It confirms the claimant will get paid, but the insurer gets recovery rights against the owner. The insurer will cite it to argue breach is fundamental.
supporting.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to satisfy third-party awards even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Invalid driving licence case. The Delhi High Court confirmed the insurer must pay third parties and recover from the owner/driver.
supporting.why_it_matters: Strong authority for the proposition that the claimant gets paid regardless of the licence defect. The insurer will cite it to establish the breach, but the ratio supports the claimant's right to payment.
supporting.quote: In view of the above discussion, there is no manner of doubt that the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Even if a fundamental breach of policy conditions is proved, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured, unless fraud or collusion is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench of Karnataka High Court — binding authority that pay-and-recover applies even for fundamental breaches like no licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most comprehensive statement of the law in the corpus. It confirms the claimant's right to payment even in the worst-case breach scenario.
supporting.quote: The Insurer is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149 (2), even if it is a fundamental breach.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had no valid licence. The court applied S. Iyyapan and directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the consistent line of authority that the third-party claimant is protected.
supporting.quote: The Hon'ble Supreme Court... has held that even if the offending vehicle was being driven by the driver having no valid driving license, insurer is liable to pay compensation to the claimants and further insurer has a right to recover the amount of compensation from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence has lapsed and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the driver does not hold a valid licence on the date of accident, but the insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Expired licence case — analogous to no valid licence. The court directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the insurer proves the licence was invalid, the third-party claimant still gets paid.
supporting.quote: The liability is fastened on the owner of the offending Maruthi Omni Car, however, the Insurance Company is directed to pay the awarded sum to the claimants and then to recover the said sum from the insured in the same proceedings by applying the principle of 'Pay and Recover'.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle, if the driver held a valid LMV licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: Supreme Court held that even if there is a licence defect (missing endorsement), the insurer must pay third parties.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the Supreme Court's most recent and authoritative statement in the corpus on the insurer's liability to third parties despite licence defects. The insurer will try to distinguish it (missing endorsement vs no licence), but the ratio on statutory liability is broad.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. result.question: What precedents could the insurance company use AGAINST our client, where the driver had no valid licence? Assess how damaging each one is.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. However, the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner (pay-and-recover).
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: driver had no licence at all. The tribunal found fundamental breach but ordered pay-and-recover to protect the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest precedent on facts — no licence whatsoever. It confirms the claimant will get paid, but the insurer gets recovery rights against the owner. The insurer will cite it to argue breach is fundamental.
supporting.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to satisfy third-party awards even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Invalid driving licence case. The Delhi High Court confirmed the insurer must pay third parties and recover from the owner/driver.
supporting.why_it_matters: Strong authority for the proposition that the claimant gets paid regardless of the licence defect. The insurer will cite it to establish the breach, but the ratio supports the claimant's right to payment.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Even if a fundamental breach of policy conditions is proved, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured, unless fraud or collusion is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench of Karnataka High Court — binding authority that pay-and-recover applies even for fundamental breaches like no licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most comprehensive statement of the law in the corpus. It confirms the claimant's right to payment even in the worst-case breach scenario.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had no valid licence. The court applied S. Iyyapan and directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the consistent line of authority that the third-party claimant is protected.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence has lapsed and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the driver does not hold a valid licence on the date of accident, but the insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Expired licence case — analogous to no valid licence. The court directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the insurer proves the licence was invalid, the third-party claimant still gets paid.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle, if the driver held a valid LMV licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: Supreme Court held that even if there is a licence defect (missing endorsement), the insurer must pay third parties.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the Supreme Court's most recent and authoritative statement in the corpus on the insurer's liability to third parties despite licence defects. The insurer will try to distinguish it (missing endorsement vs no licence), but the ratio on statutory liability is broad.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The Swaran Singh pay-and-recover principle applies ONLY to third-party risks under Section 149. It does NOT apply to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that if our client's claim is for OWN damage (comprehensive policy claim for vehicle damage, not third-party injury/death), the insurer has NO liability at all — not even pay-and-recover. The Supreme Court expressly held that Swaran Singh has no application to non-third-party claims. This is the single most dangerous precedent in the corpus for our client.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable if our client's claim is a third-party claim (injury/death to a person). The Supreme Court in Laxmi Narain Dhut itself drew a sharp distinction: for third-party risks, the insurer must pay and recover; for own-damage claims, the insurer is completely exonerated. If our client is a third-party claimant (not the owner claiming own damage), this case actually supports our position. We must confirm the nature of the claim immediately.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Driving without a licence can be treated as contributory negligence, reducing the claimant's compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that if our client (the claimant) was driving without a licence at the time of the accident, the compensation should be reduced for contributory negligence. In Kamal, the tribunal deducted 50% because the injured rider had no licence and no helmet. This could substantially reduce the award.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This applies only if our client was the driver of the vehicle (not a passenger or pedestrian). If our client was a third party (e.g., pedestrian, passenger in another vehicle), contributory negligence does not arise from the other driver's lack of licence. We must establish the factual position of our client.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that the breach is 'fundamental' — meaning the owner was grossly negligent in allowing an unlicensed driver. This strengthens the insurer's case for recovery rights against the owner and may influence the tribunal to impose the full burden on the owner. It also supports the insurer's argument that the owner acted wilfully, which could affect the scope of recovery. While the claimant still gets paid, the finding of fundamental breach makes it harder for the owner to resist the insurer's recovery, potentially leaving the claimant with a judgment that is harder to enforce if the owner is impecunious.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The tribunal still ordered pay-and-recover — the claimant got paid. The finding of 'fundamental breach' affects the owner's liability to reimburse the insurer, not the claimant's right to receive compensation. The claimant's position is that the insurer must pay first; the fight over 'fundamental breach' is between the insurer and the owner.
adverse.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle.

adverse.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
adverse.principle: Where the driver had an LMV/transport licence but no specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle, the insurer must pay and recover. However, the court also discussed Ram Babu Tiwari where the insurer was completely exonerated for a licence that had expired 3 years prior.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this for two purposes: (1) to argue that licence-type mismatches are breaches, and by extension, having no licence at all is an even more serious breach; (2) to invoke the Ram Babu Tiwari principle that where a licence has been invalid for a long period, the insurer may be completely exonerated. The insurer may argue that a driver who never had a licence is analogous to a licence that expired years ago and was never renewed.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still ordered pay-and-recover in Chennamma itself. The Ram Babu Tiwari case (cited within) involved a licence that had expired 3 years prior — the court found the owner had not taken reasonable care. But the Supreme Court in S. Iyyapan (doc_032) has since clarified that even for licence defects, the insurer must pay third parties. Chennamma's own ratio supports pay-and-recover for third-party claims.
adverse.quote: In the present case the vehicle involved in the accident is a 'heavy goods vehicle'. The driver had licence to drive 'light motor vehicle/transport vehicle'. He did not have a valid driving licence to drive 'heavy goods vehicle'.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a passenger is carried for hire/reward in a private vehicle, the insurer is completely exonerated — no pay-and-recover order can be passed because the risk is not covered by the Act policy.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may try to analogise: if the risk (passenger for hire in a private vehicle) is not covered at all, the insurer has no liability. They might argue that if the driver had no licence, the risk was never one the insurer agreed to cover, and therefore no pay-and-recover should apply. This is a creative but weak argument.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about the TYPE of risk (passenger for hire in a private vehicle) not being covered by the Act at all — a fundamentally different issue from a licence breach. The Supreme Court in Swaran Singh and S. Iyyapan has consistently held that licence breaches do NOT take the risk outside the scope of Section 147 coverage; the insurer must still pay third parties. Sukumarbai is distinguishable on this basis.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: For gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles (risk not covered by statute or policy), the Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4)/(5) to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: Similar to doc_028 — the insurer may argue by analogy that if the risk is outside the scope of the policy, no pay-and-recover can be ordered. They might argue that an unlicensed driver creates a risk that was never underwritten.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Same as doc_028. The Supreme Court in Swaran Singh and S. Iyyapan has consistently held that licence breaches are within the scope of Section 149(2) defences — the insurer can raise them as defences but must still pay third parties. Gratuitous passenger cases are about risks NOT covered by Section 147 at all — a different legal basis.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: Where a driver lacks a mandatory special endorsement (e.g., for hazardous goods), there is a breach of policy conditions entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that any licence defect — even a missing endorsement — constitutes a breach. The principle extends to 'no licence' cases by analogy: if a missing endorsement is a breach, then having no licence at all is certainly a breach. However, the court still ordered pay-and-recover, so this is low risk.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still ordered pay-and-recover — the claimants were paid. The case actually supports the claimant's right to payment. The breach finding only affects the insurer's recovery rights against the owner.
adverse.quote: Therefore, the insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
adverse.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the required badge/authorisation, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that licence defects (including no licence) constitute breaches. The case also discusses the insurer's burden of proof — the insurer successfully discharged it here, which the insurer will use to argue that if they prove the breach, they get recovery rights.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court ordered pay-and-recover — the claimant was paid. The case supports the claimant's right to payment. The breach finding only matters for the insurer's recovery against the owner.

adverse.title: Reserved On: 21.07.2025 vs State Of H.P
adverse.principle: The absence of a driving licence does not in itself constitute rashness or negligence in driving. However, driving without a licence is an offence under Section 181 MV Act.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that the driver's lack of licence is a statutory violation, reinforcing the breach argument. However, the main holding (no presumption of negligence from lack of licence) actually helps the claimant by severing the causal link between the licence defect and the accident.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a criminal revision, not a civil compensation case. The principle that 'no licence ≠ negligence' actually helps the claimant — the insurer must still prove that the accident was caused by the driver's negligence, not just that the driver had no licence.
adverse.quote: The accused cannot be held to be negligent merely because he did not possess any driving licence.

priority_arguments: 1. The claimant is a third party and the insurer's statutory liability under Section 149 MV Act is unaffected by the driver's lack of a licence — the insurer must pay and recover (S. Iyyapan, Satto, Yallavva, Meena).
2. The absence of a driving licence does not constitute negligence per se — the insurer must still prove the accident was caused by the driver's negligence (State of H.P. v. ..., doc_016).
3. Even if the breach is 'fundamental', the third-party claimant's right to payment is protected — the fight over breach is between the insurer and the owner (Sunil Shreesail Killiket, Yallavva FB).
4. If the claim is for third-party injury/death (not own damage), Laxmi Narain Dhut actually supports the claimant — it limits the insurer's complete exoneration to own-damage claims only.
